The music inside the ballroom swelled again, a string quartet hidden behind a bank of white lilies resuming their performance as if nothing had happened. Vanessa tossed her head back, her diamond earrings catching the light as she walked away from my wheelchair, her arm linking gracefully through my cousin Daniel’s. I watched them from beneath my eyelashes, tracking every subtle movement. Daniel whispered something into her ear that made her cover her mouth with a delicate laugh—a laugh that had once sounded like music to me, but now sounded like glass scraping across stone.

For three years, I had believed Daniel was my closest confidant. He was the one who managed my personal accounts, the one who sat beside me during turbulent board meetings, the one I trusted when my father passed away and left me at the helm of Sterling Enterprises. Yet, as I sat there draped in my blanket, replaying the way his eyes had slid away when Vanessa humiliated me, the truth hardened inside my chest. He wasn't just standing by; he was complicit.

Across the room, my uncle Martin was deep in conversation with Arthur Sterling, our primary competitor in the commercial real estate sector. Martin’s expression was animated, his hands cutting through the air as he pointed toward my direction. I didn't need to hear their words to know what currency they were trading. My supposed disability had opened a window of opportunity for them. They thought the crown was riderless, and they were already carving up the kingdom.

Clara had quietly stepped back, melting into the shadows near the service doors, but her presence lingered in my mind like a steady flame in a drafty room. While everyone else wore masks of polished silver and calculated indifference, she had offered a genuine human touch. A housemaid, treated like furniture by the rest of the household, possessed more integrity than anyone sharing my bloodline.

I closed my eyes for a fraction of a second, feeling the smooth leather of the wheelchair armrests beneath my fingers. My legs were strong, fully capable of carrying me across this marble floor, of standing tall and shattering every smug illusion in this room. But patience was a weapon. If I stood up now, Vanessa would scream, Daniel would look panicked, and they would scramble to cover their tracks. I needed them to walk further into the trap they were building for themselves. I needed them to sign their own professional and moral death warrants.

"Arthur," I said softly, my voice carrying just enough across the immediate space as my uncle approached my chair with a heavy, paternal hand resting on my shoulder.

"Feeling tired, nephew?" Martin asked, his voice dripping with false sympathy. "Maybe it’s time we had Clara wheel you up to your suite. You know how easily exhausted you get these days."

I looked up at him, letting a dull, vacant fatigue coat my expression. "I'm just observing, Uncle. It's fascinating watching people celebrate an ending before the book is even finished."

Martin’s smile twitched for a fraction of a second. His fingers tightened on my shoulder before he forced a hearty laugh. "Always the philosopher, Julian. But let's be realistic. Tomorrow’s emergency board meeting is going to require a lot of focus. Daniel and I have already prepared the interim leadership transition documents. You won't need to worry about a thing."

"Transition documents," I repeated slowly. "Before the doctors have even discharged me from physical therapy?"

"We're just looking out for your interests, Julian," Daniel chimed in, having walked over to join us, his tie slightly loosened. "The shareholders are nervous. The stock dipped two points this morning. We have to stabilize the company."

"Of course," I replied, maintaining a blank, submissive stare. "Run the company, Daniel. Just make sure you leave the keys in the ignition."

Daniel smirked, clearly believing my spirit was completely broken. "Rest easy, Julian. We've got everything under control."

As they walked away, laughing quietly among themselves, I looked back toward the service door where Clara stood. She caught my gaze across the crowded room. She didn't look away this time. She gave me a tiny, imperceptible nod—a silent anchor in a storm of vipers. The performance was underway, and the first act was coming to a close.
